tool.name: Numba
tool.tagline: JIT compiler that turns numeric Python and NumPy code into fast machine code
tool.description: Numba is a just-in-time compiler for Python that uses LLVM to compile functions working on numbers and NumPy arrays into native machine code. Adding a decorator such as @njit to a loop-heavy function often makes it run at C speed, with optional multithreading and custom ufuncs. It is used in scientific computing, simulation and data processing wherever a loop cannot be vectorized cleanly.

glossary.def: A Python library that compiles chosen Python functions into fast machine code the first time they are called, often making loops over numbers and arrays run as fast as compiled C.
Numba's normal way of compiling: the whole function is turned into machine code and never hands work back to the Python interpreter. @njit always uses it.
In Numba, a small compiled function that does the heavy number-crunching on arrays, while the rest of the program stays ordinary Python.
In Numba, a value that holds other values: a list, tuple, dict or array. Inside compiled code a container must hold a single type. (Not the Docker kind of container.)
The combination of argument types a compiled function accepts, such as 'a 1D float64 array and a float64'. Each distinct signature gets its own compiled version.
A signature you write out in the decorator, such as @njit("float64(float64[:])"), so the function is compiled right away and only accepts those types.
The object that @njit gives back in place of your function. On each call it looks at the argument types and runs the matching compiled version, compiling a new one if needed.
Calling a compiled function once before timing it, so that the one-off compile cost is paid and later calls measure only the running time.
The text such as '(n),()->(n)' given to @guvectorize that says which dimensions each input and output has; NumPy loops over any extra dimensions.
An ordinary Python list passed into compiled code, which Numba copies into a compiled form on each call and back afterwards. Slow and deprecated; use numba.typed.List instead.
Numba's replacement for range inside an @njit(parallel=True) function: it marks a loop whose iterations may run at the same time on several processor cores.
A loop that combines every element into one value, such as a total, a product or a maximum. Numba can split a reduction across threads and combine the partial results.
The library Numba uses underneath to start and manage threads for parallel loops: TBB, OpenMP or its own simple 'workqueue'.
Running a piece of code through the Python interpreter, with values as ordinary Python objects, from inside compiled code. Slow, but it can call anything Python can.
A widely used compiler toolkit that turns a generic description of a function into optimised machine code for the actual processor. Numba hands it the typed version of your function.
A simplified, language-neutral form of a program that a compiler works on between reading the source and producing machine code.
Numba's own intermediate representation of a function, built from the Python bytecode. Type inference and Numba's rewrite passes work on it.
LLVM's intermediate representation: the typed, low-level form Numba produces from Numba IR and hands to LLVM to optimise and turn into machine code.
The Numba Runtime: the small library compiled code uses to hand out and free memory for arrays, keeping a reference count for each one.
Wrapping a raw value such as a number or array data in a Python object (boxing) or pulling it back out (unboxing). The dispatcher does this at the boundary between Python and compiled code.
The loop nested inside another loop. Its body runs the most times, so it matters most for speed and should walk values that sit next to each other in memory.
A Numba decorator that compiles a function so C code can call it directly, giving you a raw function pointer to hand to C libraries or SciPy.
The agreed way C functions receive arguments and return results. A function compiled with it can be called straight from C code, without Python in between.
The error Numba raises when it cannot work out a type for every value in a function, usually because of an unsupported operation or a variable that takes two different types.

concepts.name: What Numba does: @njit
concepts.summary: Add @njit above a function that works on numbers and Numba turns it into fast machine code the first time you call it.
concepts.why: It is the cheapest way to make a slow Python loop over numbers run as fast as compiled code, without leaving Python.
concepts.body:
When you run ordinary Python, the interpreter works through your code one small step at a time. Before every `+` or `*` it checks what kind of value it is holding, picks the right operation, and wraps the result in a new Python object. A loop over a million numbers repeats that bookkeeping a million times, which is why plain Python loops are slow.

A **compiler** takes a different route. It translates a whole function, once, into **machine code**: the raw instructions your computer's processor runs directly, with no interpreter in between. When the types of all the values are known in advance, there is nothing left to check at each step, so the same loop can run tens or hundreds of times faster.

**Numba** is a compiler for Python that works *just in time*. A **JIT compiler** does not compile your whole program up front; it compiles a function the first time that function is called, using the types of the arguments it was given. Later calls with the same kinds of arguments jump straight into the compiled version.

You switch it on with a decorator. The one you will use most is `@njit`, short for `@jit(nopython=True)`. In **nopython mode** the whole function is compiled and never hands work back to the interpreter, which is where the speed comes from. Since Numba 0.59, plain `@jit` also defaults to nopython mode, so the two behave the same; `@njit` is still the common spelling.

Numba works best on code that:

- loops over NumPy arrays or ranges of numbers,
- uses single numbers, tuples, NumPy arrays and a subset of Python and NumPy functions,
- would be awkward or memory-hungry to write as vectorized NumPy.

A small compiled function like this, which does the heavy number-crunching while the rest of your program stays ordinary Python, is often called a **kernel**. Numba does not speed up code that calls pandas, does string-heavy work or passes around general Python objects; such code fails to compile in nopython mode with a `TypingError`.

The decorated function is still called like any Python function: pass it arrays and numbers as usual. The original, uncompiled version is kept as `func.py_func`, which is handy for checking that both give the same answer.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
from numba import njit

@njit
def sum_of_squares(a):
    total = 0.0
    for x in a:           # a plain loop, compiled to machine code
        total += x * x
    return total

a = np.arange(1_000_000, dtype=np.float64)
print(sum_of_squares(a))           # 3.3333283333312755e+17
print(sum_of_squares.py_func(a[:4]))  # 14.0 (the original Python function)
print(sum_of_squares(a[:4]))       # 14.0
takeaways: @njit compiles a function to machine code on its first call
Nopython mode means no interpreter in the loop: that is where the speed comes from
func.py_func is the original Python function
pitfalls: Decorating code that uses pandas or general Python objects and expecting it to compile.

quiz.q: Why does a Numba-compiled loop run much faster than the same pure Python loop?
options: It runs the loop on the graphics card
The types are known, so it runs machine code instead of interpreting each step
It remembers the result of the previous call
quiz.explain: Because Numba knows the type of every value, it can produce machine code that works on plain numbers directly, with no per-step checking by the interpreter.

concepts.name: Compilation, warm-up and caching
concepts.summary: The first call is slow because it compiles; learn to time the right call, and keep compiled code on disk with cache=True.
concepts.why: Mistaking the one-off compile time for the running time is the most common reason people think Numba 'didn't help'.
concepts.body:
Numba compiles **lazily, on the first call** with a new combination of argument types. That first call does all the work: working out the type of every variable, optimising, and producing machine code. It can take from a fraction of a second to several seconds for a big function. Every later call with the same types reuses the compiled machine code and is fast.

So measure correctly. Call the function once first so that it compiles (people say you **warm it up**), then time the later calls, for example with `timeit` or `time.perf_counter`. If you time the first call you are measuring the compiler, not your code.

The combination of argument types a function was called with is its **signature**, for example 'a 1D array of float64 and a float64'. Each distinct signature gets its own compiled version: calling with an `int64` array and later a `float32` array compiles twice. The object that `@njit` gives you back is called the **dispatcher**; on each call it looks at the argument types and picks (or compiles) the matching version. Its `signatures` attribute lists what has been compiled so far.

Compiled code is kept only in memory, so it is gone when your program ends. If a script starts often, pass `cache=True`: Numba saves the compiled code in a `__pycache__` folder next to your `.py` file and loads it the next time the program starts, as long as the file and the Numba version are unchanged. Caching only works for functions written in a file, not ones typed into the REPL.

If compile time matters, prefer fewer, larger compiled functions over many tiny ones, and keep the dtypes of your inputs consistent so nothing has to be compiled twice.
concepts.code:
import time
import numpy as np
from numba import njit

@njit(cache=True)
def clip_sum(a, lo, hi):
    s = 0.0
    for x in a:
        s += min(max(x, lo), hi)
    return s

a = np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=2_000_000)

t = time.perf_counter(); clip_sum(a, -1.0, 1.0)
print(f"first call:  {time.perf_counter() - t:.3f}s")  # includes compiling (or loading the cache)
t = time.perf_counter(); clip_sum(a, -1.0, 1.0)
print(f"second call: {time.perf_counter() - t:.3f}s")  # run time only, e.g. 0.002s

clip_sum(a.astype(np.float32), -1.0, 1.0)   # new dtype -> compiles again
print(len(clip_sum.signatures))             # 2
takeaways: The first call for each signature compiles; later calls are fast
Warm up before timing
cache=True saves compiled code on disk for the next run
pitfalls: Timing only the first call and concluding Numba is slow.

quiz.q: A function is called with a float64 array, then an int32 array, then a float64 array again. How many times is it compiled?
quiz.explain: One compilation per distinct signature: float64 and int32. The third call reuses the float64 version.

concepts.name: What nopython mode supports
concepts.summary: Know which Python features and NumPy functions compile in nopython mode, and what to do about the rest.
concepts.why: Writing inside the supported subset from the start saves you from fighting compiler errors later.
concepts.body:
Numba compiles a **subset** of Python and NumPy: a well-chosen part of each, not everything. Inside an `@njit` function you can use:

- numbers (`int`, `float`, `complex`, `bool`), `None`, tuples and named tuples,
- `if`, `for`, `while`, `break`, `continue`, `range`, `enumerate`, `zip`,
- NumPy arrays of numeric, boolean and some datetime dtypes, with indexing, slicing, views and most arithmetic,
- a large part of NumPy: creation functions (`np.zeros`, `np.empty`, `np.arange`), the maths ufuncs, aggregations (`sum`, `mean`, `argmax`), `np.sort`, `np.linalg` and the older-style `np.random` functions,
- the `math` and `cmath` modules, strings with basic operations, lists and dicts that hold one type, sets, simple classes via `@jitclass`, and calls to other `@njit` functions.

What does **not** work: pandas, most of the standard library, general Python objects (anything that is not a number, tuple, array or one of the collections above), `try`/`except` beyond simple cases, lists or dicts that mix types, and many keyword arguments of NumPy functions (for example `dtype=` or `axis=` support varies from function to function).

A **container** here means a value that holds other values: a list, tuple or dict. Inside compiled code a container must hold a single type: a list of floats is fine; `[1, "a"]` is a typing error. Arrays are the preferred container, because an array is one unbroken block of numbers in memory that compiled code can work through directly.

When something is unsupported, the usual fix is to reorganise: read files and do pandas work outside, then pass plain NumPy arrays into a small compiled kernel. Numba's reference pages list the supported Python features and NumPy functions in detail.
takeaways: Numbers, tuples, loops, NumPy arrays and much of NumPy compile
A list or dict must hold a single type
Keep pandas, file reading and general objects outside; pass arrays into compiled kernels
pitfalls: Assuming every keyword argument of a NumPy function is supported inside @njit.

quiz.q: Which of these will compile inside an @njit function?
options: A list holding both ints and strings
quiz.explain: NumPy ufuncs and aggregations are supported; pandas, mixed-type lists and most of the standard library are not.

concepts.name: Writing fast loops over arrays
concepts.summary: Write plain index loops over NumPy arrays, create the output array up front, and walk through memory in order for Numba speed.
concepts.why: Plain loops are Numba's strength, and a few habits decide whether they run at full speed.
concepts.body:
With Numba, the loop you would avoid in plain Python becomes the fastest option. A typical compiled kernel is simple: create the output array once with `np.empty`, loop over the indexes, and write each result into its place.

Habits that keep loops fast:

- **Create arrays once, up front** (people say *preallocate*) instead of appending to a list and converting at the end.
- **Loop in the order values sit in memory.** A computer reads memory fastest when the values it needs are next to each other. In a row-major (C order) 2D array a row is stored as one run of values, so make the last index the **inner loop** (the loop nested inside the other, whose body runs most often): `for i in range(n): for j in range(m): a[i, j]`. An inner loop that jumps from row to row throws that advantage away.
- **Keep each variable one type.** Start a running total with the right type (`0.0` for floats, `0` for integers). A variable that is an integer on one branch and a float on another forces Numba to pick a type that fits both, which can block optimisations.
- **Avoid making small arrays inside the loop.** `a[i:i+3].sum()` inside a loop creates a new array object and calls a function on every pass; a short inner loop over the three values is usually faster.
- **Do several things in one pass.** Compute several statistics in one loop instead of calling `mean`, then `std`, then `max`, each of which reads the whole array again.

Loops where each step depends on an earlier one are where Numba beats NumPy: a running sum that resets, a formula like `y[i] = a * y[i-1] + x[i]` where each value is built from the previous one, logic that changes behaviour depending on what came before, or a search that stops as soon as it finds a match. These either cannot be vectorized or need several extra full-size arrays in NumPy.

Arrays passed in are not copied: writing to them inside the function changes the caller's array, just as in Python.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
from numba import njit

@njit
def ewma(x, alpha):
    # y[i] depends on y[i-1]: hard to vectorize, easy to loop
    y = np.empty_like(x)
    y[0] = x[0]
    for i in range(1, x.size):
        y[i] = alpha * x[i] + (1 - alpha) * y[i - 1]
    return y

@njit
def row_sums(a):
    out = np.zeros(a.shape[0])
    for i in range(a.shape[0]):        # outer: rows
        for j in range(a.shape[1]):    # inner: values of one row, side by side in memory
            out[i] += a[i, j]
    return out

print(ewma(np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]), 0.5))  # [1.    1.5   2.25  3.125]
print(row_sums(np.arange(6.0).reshape(2, 3)))     # [ 3. 12.]
takeaways: Create output arrays up front and write by index
Make the innermost loop walk values that sit next to each other in memory
Loops where each step depends on the previous one are where loops beat vectorized NumPy
pitfalls: Making the inner loop jump between rows of a row-major array.

quiz.q: For a row-major (C order) array a of shape (n, m), which loop order is faster in Numba?
options: for j over columns outside, for i over rows inside
Whichever loop is written with while
for i over rows outside, for j over columns inside
quiz.explain: In row-major order each row is stored as one run of values, so the inner loop should walk along a row.

concepts.name: Type inference and explicit signatures
concepts.summary: See how Numba works out types, read compiled signatures, and give explicit ones to compile up front.
concepts.why: Most Numba errors and slowdowns are type problems, so you need to see what the compiler decided.
concepts.body:
Numba's types carry more than NumPy dtypes do. An array type records **dtype, number of dimensions and layout**, written like `float64[:, ::1]` (2D, with each row stored as one unbroken run in memory: C-contiguous) or `int32[:]` (1D, any layout). Single values are `int64`, `float64`, `boolean`, `complex128`, and so on. Every variable in a compiled function gets exactly one type, chosen so that every assignment to it fits.

Normally the dispatcher compiles lazily for whatever arguments it sees. You can instead pass **explicit signatures** to compile up front, when the decorator runs:

```python
@njit("float64(float64[:], float64)")
```

or with type objects, `@njit(float64(float64[::1], float64))`. With signatures, only those types are accepted; calling with anything else raises `TypeError` instead of compiling a new version. Signatures are useful for warming up before the program really starts, for libraries that want predictable behaviour, and for `cfunc` and `@vectorize`, which require them.

To inspect what happened:

- `f.signatures` lists the compiled signatures.
- `numba.typeof(value)` shows the Numba type of a Python value.
- `f.inspect_types()` prints the source with the type of every variable written next to it, revealing surprises such as an `int64` that became a `float64`, or `pyobject`, which means Numba gave up on typing that value.

Integers behave differently from Python: a Numba integer has a fixed size (`int64` by default, 64 bits), so a result too big for it silently wraps around instead of growing without limit like a Python int.
takeaways: Array types include dtype, number of dimensions and layout (C, F or A)
Explicit signatures compile up front and reject other types
Numba integers have a fixed size and can overflow silently
pitfalls: Assuming Python's unlimited integers inside compiled code.

quiz.q: A function is decorated with @njit('float64(float64[:])'). What happens when it is called with an int64 array?
options: It compiles a new int64 version
It raises a TypeError: no matching definition
It falls back to Python mode
quiz.explain: With explicit signatures the dispatcher only accepts those types and does not compile new ones.

concepts.name: @vectorize and @guvectorize ufuncs
concepts.summary: Write a function for single values and turn it into a real NumPy ufunc with broadcasting, or a generalized ufunc that works on whole rows.
concepts.why: Custom ufuncs plug into NumPy broadcasting and aggregations while running compiled code.
concepts.body:
`@vectorize` takes a function written for **single values** (scalars) and builds a true NumPy ufunc from it. The ufunc then works on single values and on arrays of any shape, with full **broadcasting**, `out=` arguments and ufunc methods such as `.reduce` and `.accumulate`.

```python
@vectorize(["float64(float64, float64)"])
def rel_diff(x, y): ...
```

With a list of signatures, the ufunc is compiled up front for those types. Without signatures you get a dynamic ufunc that compiles a new version each time it meets a new type. The `target` option selects `"cpu"` (the default: one core) or `"parallel"` (spread the work across several processor cores; worth it only for large arrays).

`@guvectorize` builds a **generalized ufunc**: a ufunc that works on whole sub-arrays, such as rows, rather than on single values. You describe the shapes with a layout string like `"(n),()->(n)"`, meaning 'a 1D run of length n and a single value in, a 1D run of length n out'. The function receives array slices and writes its result into the output argument (it does not `return`). NumPy loops over the remaining leading dimensions for you, so a function written for one row automatically applies to every row of a 2D array.

Compared with `@njit`, ufuncs give you NumPy behaviour for free: broadcasting rules, picking the right compiled version for each dtype, and working with code that expects ufuncs. Use `@njit` when elements depend on each other, for example when each value is built from the previous one, which a ufunc cannot express.
takeaways: @vectorize turns a function for single values into a broadcasting NumPy ufunc
@guvectorize works on sub-arrays described by a layout string and writes to an output argument
Use @njit when elements depend on each other
pitfalls: Returning a value from a @guvectorize function instead of filling the output argument.

quiz.q: What does a @guvectorize function with layout '(n)->()' applied to a (5, 3) array return?
quiz.explain: Each call consumes one run of n=3 values and gives one result; NumPy loops over the leading dimension of size 5.

concepts.name: Typed List and Dict
concepts.summary: Use numba.typed.List and numba.typed.Dict for single-type lists and dictionaries inside compiled code.
concepts.why: Algorithms that need growing collections or lookup tables can stay fully compiled.
concepts.body:
Arrays have a fixed size, but many algorithms need a list that grows or a dictionary for lookups: collecting each node's neighbours in a graph, counting how often values occur, remembering results already computed. Numba provides compiled, single-type versions in `numba.typed`:

- `typed.List`: a list whose items all have one type. You can create one in Python (`List()` then `append`, or `List([1.0, 2.0])`) and pass it into compiled functions, or create a list inside an `@njit` function with an ordinary `[]` and `append`.
- `typed.Dict`: a dictionary whose keys all have one type and whose values all have one type. Create it empty with explicit types, `Dict.empty(key_type=types.int64, value_type=types.float64)`, or inside compiled code with `{}` and assignments, where the types are taken from the first item you insert.

Every item and key must have the same Numba type. Values can be numbers, tuples, arrays (as long as all have the same dtype and number of dimensions) or other typed containers.

Why not just pass a Python list? Numba used to support ordinary Python lists by copying them into a compiled form on every call and back afterwards (so-called **reflected lists**), which was slow and is deprecated. Typed containers live in memory that compiled code manages, so they pass into and out of compiled functions without any conversion. Using them from plain Python, however, is slower than a normal list, because every access goes through a compiled helper. Treat them as the containers for compiled code, not as a general replacement.

Typed dicts and lists are usable from both sides, so you can build data in a compiled function and inspect it in Python.
takeaways: typed.List and typed.Dict hold one Numba type per container
Create them in Python or with [] and {} inside @njit code
They are for compiled code; plain Python access is slower than the built-ins
pitfalls: Passing a regular Python list of lists into @njit code (reflected lists are deprecated and slow).

quiz.q: Which value can be inserted into Dict.empty(key_type=types.int64, value_type=types.float64)?
quiz.explain: Keys must be int64 and values float64; strings and tuples have other types.

concepts.name: Numba vs NumPy vs others
concepts.summary: Decide when Numba beats vectorized NumPy, when it does not help, and what the alternatives are.
concepts.why: Adding @njit everywhere wastes compile time; knowing where it wins focuses the effort.
concepts.body:
Vectorized NumPy already runs compiled loops written in C, so wrapping a single NumPy call such as `a.sum()` in `@njit` gives no speedup: Numba generates comparable code. The same goes for `a @ b`: matrix products are handed either way to **BLAS**, the long-established, heavily tuned maths library that NumPy uses for linear algebra.

Numba wins when NumPy would need **several passes or temporary arrays** (full-size intermediate arrays made for one step of an expression and then thrown away), or when the algorithm is inherently step by step:

- Expressions such as `np.sqrt(x**2 + y**2) * np.exp(-z)`, where NumPy makes a new array for every operation. A Numba loop does it all in one pass with no temporaries.
- Loops where each value depends on the previous one, logic that changes with what came before, early exits, and searches.
- Algorithms that jump around memory in data-dependent ways: graphs, histograms with custom bins, particle simulations, table-filling algorithms such as edit distance.
- Code that would otherwise need `np.vectorize` (which is just a Python loop in disguise) or Python-level loops around NumPy calls.

Numba does not help with code that mostly waits for files or the network, with pandas or string processing, or with code dominated by calls to large NumPy or BLAS routines.

Alternatives to know:

- **Cython**: compiled in advance, before the program runs; good for wrapping C libraries and distributing ready-built packages, but more setup.
- **JAX**: array programming that can compute derivatives automatically and run on GPUs, written in a functional style.
- **NumExpr**: evaluates array expressions in one pass without you writing loops.
- For GPUs, Numba's support for NVIDIA cards now lives in the separate `numba-cuda` package maintained by NVIDIA.

Measure first: profile, find the function that takes the time, then decide.
concepts.code:
import time
import numpy as np
from numba import njit

x = np.random.default_rng(1).random(5_000_000)

def numpy_version(x):
    return np.sqrt(x**2 + 1.0) * np.exp(-x)   # several temporary arrays

@njit
def numba_version(x):
    out = np.empty_like(x)
    for i in range(x.size):                    # one fused pass, no temporaries
        out[i] = np.sqrt(x[i] ** 2 + 1.0) * np.exp(-x[i])
    return out

numba_version(x[:10])                          # warm up
for f in (numpy_version, numba_version):
    t = time.perf_counter(); f(x)
    print(f.__name__, f"{time.perf_counter() - t:.3f}s")
print(np.allclose(numpy_version(x), numba_version(x)))  # True
takeaways: Single NumPy calls are already compiled; wrapping them in @njit gains nothing
Numba wins on fused expressions, step-by-step loops and irregular algorithms
Profile first; consider Cython, JAX or NumExpr where they fit better
pitfalls: Expecting @njit around a large matrix multiplication to beat NumPy's BLAS.

quiz.q: Which function is most likely to get a big speedup from @njit?
options: return a @ b for two large matrices
A loop that tracks a running maximum and resets it when a value drops below zero
quiz.explain: Step-by-step logic that carries state cannot be vectorized well; the others are already compiled or unsupported.

concepts.name: Multithreading with parallel=True and prange
concepts.summary: Run loops on all cores with parallel=True and prange, and understand reductions, races and threading layers.
concepts.why: A parallel loop can multiply speed by the number of cores with a one-word change, if the loop is safe.
concepts.body:
`@njit(parallel=True)` enables two things. First, Numba automatically spreads supported array expressions and aggregations across several processor cores. Second, you can replace `range` with `numba.prange` to mark a loop whose iterations run **in parallel threads**: separate lines of execution that the operating system runs on different cores at the same time. Python's usual rule that only one thread runs Python code at a time (the GIL) does not get in the way, because the compiled code is not Python code any more.

Rules for a correct `prange` loop:

- Iterations must be **independent**. Writing to `out[i]` from iteration `i` is safe. Writing to the same element from several iterations is a **race condition**, where two threads update it at once and one update is lost, and gives wrong results.
- A **reduction** is a loop that combines every element into one value, like a total. Numba recognises `total += f(a[i])` inside a `prange` loop and turns it into a partial sum per thread that is combined at the end. This works for `+=`, `*=` and similar operators on single values, not for arbitrary updates of array elements.
- Only the outermost `prange` in a nest is run in parallel; inner ones run one iteration after another.

Control and inspect the threading:

- `numba.set_num_threads(n)` and `get_num_threads()` change the thread count while the program runs, and the `NUMBA_NUM_THREADS` environment variable sets the maximum.
- `f.parallel_diagnostics(level=1)` reports which loops were run in parallel and which were merged.
- The **threading layer** is the library Numba uses underneath to start and manage threads (TBB, OpenMP or Numba's own simple 'workqueue'); choose it with `NUMBA_THREADING_LAYER`.

Parallel work has overhead: for small arrays or cheap loop bodies the single-thread version is faster. Floating-point reductions may also give slightly different results from the serial sum, because the order of the additions changes.
takeaways: parallel=True plus prange runs independent iterations on several cores
Reductions with += on a single value are handled; shared array writes are races
Overhead and a changed order of additions are the trade-offs
pitfalls: Updating a shared histogram bin from a prange loop, which silently loses counts.

quiz.q: Inside a prange loop over i, which update is a race condition?
options: s += a[i] where s is a scalar declared before the loop
tmp = a[i] + 1 with tmp local to the iteration
hist[a[i]] += 1 for a shared hist array
quiz.explain: Different iterations can hit the same bin at the same time, so increments are lost.

concepts.name: fastmath, boundscheck and other options
concepts.summary: Use compiler options such as fastmath, boundscheck, error_model and inline to trade strictness for speed knowingly.
concepts.why: These flags unlock faster maths and remove safety checks, but each changes behaviour in specific ways.
concepts.body:
The JIT decorators accept options that change what the compiler may assume. Numba hands your typed function to **LLVM**, a widely used compiler toolkit, to turn it into machine code; several of these options are instructions to LLVM.

- `fastmath=True` lets LLVM ignore the strict IEEE 754 rules. It may reorder additions, which allows **SIMD** instructions (processor instructions that do the same operation on several numbers at once, say 8 additions in one step) to be used for sums; it may assume there are no NaNs or infinities; and it may use faster, slightly less exact forms of division. Loops summing floats often get several times faster. The price: results can differ in the last few digits, and code that relies on NaN checks (`x != x`, `np.isnan`) may be optimised away. You can pass a set of flags such as `{"nsz", "arcp", "contract", "afn", "reassoc"}` to enable only some relaxations, leaving NaN and infinity handling intact.
- `boundscheck=True` turns on checking that every index is inside the array. By default Numba does **not** check, so `a[10]` on a 5-element array reads or writes whatever memory happens to be there. Enable checks while debugging, or everywhere with `NUMBA_BOUNDSCHECK=1`.
- `error_model="numpy"` makes division by zero return `inf` or `nan` as NumPy does, instead of raising `ZeroDivisionError` as Python does. Removing the check makes division-heavy loops faster.
- `inline="always"` copies the body of a small `@njit` function into every place that calls it, before the code reaches LLVM; LLVM usually does this for small functions anyway.
- `nogil=True` and `cache=True` are covered elsewhere.

Treat these as measured optimisations: benchmark with and without, and compare the numerical results against the strict version.
takeaways: fastmath allows reordering and SIMD; results may change slightly and NaN checks may vanish
Indexes are not checked by default; enable boundscheck while debugging
error_model='numpy' returns inf/nan for division by zero
pitfalls: Using fastmath=True in code that tests for NaN, which may then never detect it.

quiz.q: By default, what happens in @njit code when you read a[10] from a 5-element array?
options: Nothing is checked: it reads whatever memory is there
quiz.explain: Index checking is off by default for speed; an out-of-range index is not detected.

concepts.name: Reading errors and debugging
concepts.summary: Diagnose TypingErrors, switch the JIT off to debug in plain Python, and escape to object mode for unsupported calls.
concepts.why: Numba's error messages are long; knowing how to read them and where to look saves hours.
concepts.body:
Most failures are a `TypingError` raised on the first call. The message is long, but it has a fixed structure: what operation failed (for example "No implementation of function Function(<built-in function add>) found for signature: (int64, unicode_type)"), the list of candidate implementations tried, and, at the end, the **source line** where it happened. Read the bottom first.

Common causes:

- a variable that takes two incompatible types on different branches, such as `None` and an array,
- an unsupported function or keyword argument,
- an empty list (`[]`) that is never appended to, so its item type is unknown,
- passing an unsupported object (a pandas Series, a general Python object) as an argument.

Debugging tools:

- `NUMBA_DISABLE_JIT=1` in the environment makes every Numba decorator do nothing, so you can use Python's debugger `pdb`, breakpoints and prints on the pure Python version.
- `print()` works in compiled code for simple values.
- `f.inspect_types()` shows the type Numba chose for every variable.
- `with numba.objmode(result="float64"):` runs a block in **object mode**: the interpreter runs it, with values handled as ordinary Python objects, from inside compiled code. Use it to call an unsupported library or a timer. Declare the types of the variables that leave the block. It is slow, so keep it out of hot loops.

Errors while running behave differently from Python: raising exceptions works for simple cases, but without `boundscheck` an out-of-range index is not caught, and an integer that grows too big silently wraps around. When results look wrong rather than failing, compare with `f.py_func` on a small input.
takeaways: Read a TypingError from the bottom: the failing source line is at the end
NUMBA_DISABLE_JIT=1 lets you debug the pure Python version
objmode runs a block in the interpreter with declared output types
pitfalls: Leaving objmode blocks inside hot loops, which brings back interpreter overhead.

quiz.q: A variable is assigned None in one branch and an array in another. What is the likely result?
options: A TypingError on the first call
quiz.explain: Every variable needs one unified type; Numba fails to unify these and reports a TypingError (Optional types only help in specific cases).

concepts.name: Inside the compiler: from bytecode to LLVM
concepts.summary: Follow Numba's pipeline from Python bytecode through Numba IR and type inference to LLVM IR and assembly.
concepts.why: Knowing each stage tells you where an error comes from and how to check that code was vectorized.
concepts.body:
When the dispatcher sees a new signature it runs a compilation pipeline, one stage feeding the next.

**Bytecode analysis.** Numba takes apart the function's CPython bytecode and builds a map of which blocks of code can lead to which (a control flow graph). That is why Numba support depends on the Python version: each new CPython release changes the bytecode.

**Numba IR.** The bytecode is translated into Numba's own **intermediate representation** (IR): a simplified, language-neutral form of the function that is easier to analyse than bytecode. Rewrite passes then improve it: copying small functions into their callers, computing constant expressions in advance, and for `parallel=True`, merging array expressions and splitting loops across threads.

**Type inference.** Starting from the argument types, Numba works out a type for every value in the IR, matching each operation and call to a typed implementation. Failure here is your `TypingError`.

**Lowering.** Each typed operation is turned into **LLVM IR**, LLVM's own intermediate form. Array memory is managed by calls into Numba's runtime library (NRT): each array has a reference count, and its data lives in memory that NRT hands out and frees.

**LLVM.** LLVM optimises (copying small functions into callers, turning loops into SIMD instructions, propagating constants) and generates machine code for the processor of the machine you are on. The result is linked and wrapped so Python can call it.

You can inspect each stage of a compiled function: `inspect_types()` for the typed IR, `inspect_llvm()` and `inspect_asm()` for the LLVM IR and the assembly (human-readable machine code) per signature. Searching the assembly for vector instructions such as `vaddpd` (AVX) confirms SIMD vectorization.

At the boundary, the dispatcher **unboxes** each argument (pulls the raw number or array data out of its Python object) and **boxes** the result back into a Python object, which costs a microsecond or so per call. Call compiled functions from other compiled functions to avoid it, and keep the work per call large.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
from numba import njit

@njit(fastmath=True)
def dot(a, b):
    s = 0.0
    for i in range(a.size):
        s += a[i] * b[i]
    return s

x = np.ones(1000)
print(dot(x, x))                         # 1000.0

sig = dot.signatures[0]
llvm_ir = dot.inspect_llvm(sig)
asm = dot.inspect_asm(sig)
print("fmul" in llvm_ir)                 # True: multiply in LLVM IR
print(any(op in asm for op in ("vfmadd", "vmulpd", "mulpd", "fmla")))
# True on most CPUs: SIMD instructions in the generated assembly
takeaways: Pipeline: bytecode, Numba IR, type inference, lowering to LLVM IR, machine code
inspect_types, inspect_llvm and inspect_asm show each stage
Each call from Python pays a boxing cost; keep calls coarse-grained
pitfalls: Calling a tiny compiled function millions of times from Python, where the call overhead dominates.

quiz.q: In which pipeline stage is a TypingError raised?
quiz.explain: Type inference propagates types from the arguments and fails when no typed implementation matches.

concepts.name: Releasing the GIL and C callbacks
concepts.summary: Use nogil=True to run compiled code in Python threads at the same time, and @cfunc to hand native callbacks to C libraries.
concepts.why: These are the tools for fitting Numba kernels into threaded applications and into C and SciPy APIs.
concepts.body:
Compiled nopython code does not need the interpreter, but by default it still holds the **GIL** while running, so two Python threads calling the same compiled function run one after the other. `@njit(nogil=True)` releases the GIL when the function starts and takes it back when it returns. Then a `ThreadPoolExecutor` can run several calls truly in parallel on different cores, with ordinary threads and shared memory, no `prange` needed.

You become responsible for thread safety: two threads writing the same array is a race condition, just as in C. Releasing the GIL is also not possible in object mode or inside `objmode` blocks. On free-threaded Python builds the GIL may be absent anyway, but `nogil=True` remains the explicit way to declare compiled code safe to run concurrently.

`@cfunc(signature)` compiles a function with a **C calling convention**: it takes and returns values the way a C function does, so C code can call it directly, instead of producing a dispatcher that Python calls. Its `.address` is the raw memory address of the compiled function (a function pointer) and `.ctypes` wraps it for Python's `ctypes` module. Use it to pass callbacks to C libraries: for example `scipy.integrate.quad` and `scipy.LowLevelCallable` accept such pointers, removing the cost of a Python call per evaluation, often a large speedup for integrators and optimisers. Inside a cfunc you cannot raise Python exceptions to the caller, and arguments must be C-compatible types (numbers and raw pointers; `carray` lets you view a pointer as an array).

Related: Numba's `numba.pycc` module for compiling in advance is deprecated; for shipping compiled extensions, caching or Cython are the usual routes.
concepts.code:
import ctypes
import numpy as np
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from numba import njit, cfunc, float64

@njit(nogil=True)
def heavy(a):
    s = 0.0
    for x in a:
        s += np.sin(x) ** 2
    return s

chunks = np.array_split(np.random.default_rng(0).random(4_000_000), 4)
with ThreadPoolExecutor(4) as pool:            # runs concurrently: GIL released
    print(round(sum(pool.map(heavy, chunks))))  # 1090663

@cfunc(float64(float64))
def square(x):
    return x * x

print(square.ctypes(3.0))                      # 9.0  (called through a C pointer)
print(isinstance(square.address, int))         # True
takeaways: nogil=True lets Python threads run compiled code at the same time
You are responsible for avoiding race conditions once the GIL is released
@cfunc produces a C function pointer for callbacks into C and SciPy
pitfalls: Releasing the GIL and then writing to the same output array from several threads.

quiz.q: Without nogil=True, four threads each calling an @njit function on separate data will:
options: Run in parallel on four cores
Run mostly one at a time because the GIL is held
quiz.explain: Compiled code holds the GIL by default, so threads are serialised.

concepts.name: Extending Numba with @overload
concepts.summary: Teach Numba to compile your own functions or unsupported library calls with the high-level @overload API.
concepts.why: Libraries built on Numba, and teams with shared kernels, need typed implementations of their own functions.
concepts.body:
When a function is not supported in nopython mode, you can register a compiled implementation for it with `numba.extending.overload`. The pattern has two layers:

```python
@overload(target_func)
def ol_target(x, y):          # typing time: receives Numba TYPES
    if isinstance(x, types.Array):
        def impl(x, y):       # run time: receives values
            ...
        return impl
```

The outer function runs during **type inference** with the Numba types of the arguments, not their values. It inspects the types and returns a Python function implementing the operation for them, or returns `None` to say 'not supported for these types', which lets other overloads be tried. The returned implementation is compiled like any `@njit` function. So the choice of implementation is made once, while compiling, and costs nothing while the code runs.

Related APIs:

- `@overload_method(types.Array, "name")` adds methods to Numba types.
- `@overload_attribute` adds attributes.
- `@register_jitable` is a shortcut for a function that works the same in Python and compiled code.
- `@intrinsic` is the low-level layer: you write the LLVM IR generation yourself, for operations that cannot be expressed in Python.
- The low-level extension API (`typeof_impl`, `models`, `lower_builtin`) adds entirely new types, which is how libraries teach Numba about their own objects.

Overloads are registered for the whole program when their module is imported, so import the module that defines them before compiling code that uses them.
takeaways: @overload maps a Python function to typed compiled implementations
The outer function sees types and returns an implementation (or None)
overload_method, intrinsic and the low-level API go further
pitfalls: Inspecting argument values inside the outer overload function, which only receives types.

quiz.q: What does the outer function decorated with @overload receive as arguments?
options: Numba type objects describing the arguments
quiz.explain: It runs at type-inference time and dispatches on Numba types.
